newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Leica snaps back into profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Leica snaps back into profit.

text.p: Prestigious German camera maker Leica Camera AG on Tuesday reported a return to profit in the first nine months of its 1996/1997 fiscal year amid sharp productivity gains at its main plant in Solms.

Swiss-owned Leica, which was floated on the stock market last year, said it swung to a net profit of 4.9 million marks ($3 million) in the nine months to December 31 from a loss of 1.6 million marks in the year-earlier period.
A spokesman attributed the turnaround to investment in new machinery which had significantly shortened the time it takes to produce cameras, lenses and binoculars at Solms.

Even though many of Leica's cameras are as expensive as small cars, professional photographers account for just 10 percent of sales of its two top-of-the-range models, the M6 rangefinder camera and the R8 single-lens reflex.
The rest is bought by amateur enthusiasts who are slaves to photography.
"Most of our cameras are bought by ambitious amateurs who regard photography as their number one hobby," said Leica spokesman Hans Guenther von Zydowitz.

The manual focus R8, launched before Christmas and priced at 4,400 marks excluding a lens, is selling well and Leica plans to produce 5,000 to 6,000 of them by March 31, when its 1996/1997 fiscal year ends, von Zydowitz said.
Sales of the R8 have already caught up with the M6, hitherto Leica's 4,300 mark flagship famed for its sturdy construction, lens quality and silent mechanism.
Both models now account for 24-25 percent each of Leica's sales, von Zydowitz said.
Overall, sales rose 7.1 percent to 174.8 million marks in the first nine months of 1996/1997, with earnings before income and tax rising to 5.7 million marks from 2.1 million, Leica said.

Business was boosted by the giant Photokina photographic fair in Cologne last autumn and sales jumped 14.4 percent to 76.3 million marks in the three months to end-December, with net profit up at 3.0 million from 0.5 million, Leica said.

The news failed to invigorate Leica's shares which closed down 0.20 marks at 51.80 marks in a firmer overall market. But Leica was still up 10 percent from the price of 47 marks the shares were issued at last September.
Relying on demand from photography purists who insist on equipment that gives them complete creative control, Leica has avoided equipping its top models with innovations like automatic focusing.

It also has no plans to follow its competitors into the Advanced Photo System (APS) launched last year, a new generation of film and cameras that offers a range of different picture formats from one film.

Von Zydowitz blamed the introduction of APS for unsettling prospective buyers and causing stagnation in the compact camera market last year. Leica has ventured down into that market recently with competitively priced compacts assembled in Japan.
Its new compact camera subsidiary Minox, bought last April, should reach break-even before the end of 1996/1997, Leica said.
